tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

level.description: Effort level the review ran at

findings.description: Verified findings, most-severe first; empty if none survived

file.description: Repo-relative path of the file the finding is in

short_summary.description: Compressed label for compact UI (≤60 chars): the claim alone, no rationale or consequence clause

category.description: Short kebab-case slug of the finding type, e.g. "correctness", "simplification", "efficiency", "test-coverage"

verdict.description: Set when a verify pass ran; absent on inline-only reviews

outcome.description: Set ONLY when re-reporting after applying fixes: what happened to this finding

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

type.description: What kind of feedback this is.

title.description: Short, specific one-line summary of the issue.

details.description: Labeled bullets, in order: **What happened:** (observed vs. expected, exact error text if short); **What the user said:** (quoted, or "User didn't comment; observed by the model."); **Repro:** (minimal steps); **Evidence:** (request IDs, timestamps, paths, versions; omit if none); optionally a final **Cause:** only if verified in-session. One to three lines per bullet. No narrative paragraphs, no speculation, no secrets.

area.description: Optional short tag naming the part of Claude Code this is about (e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing"). Leave blank if unclear.

failure_mode.description: When the report is about MODEL BEHAVIOR (not a product bug), the closest failure mode, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value. Omit only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.

task_category.description: What kind of task the session was doing when the issue occurred, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: WebFetch
tools.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead. claude.ai artifact links (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}) are published artifacts: read them with the Artifact tool (action "read"), not WebFetch or curl.
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

url.description: The URL to fetch content from

prompt.description: The prompt to run on the fetched content

offset.description: Character position in the page text to start reading from. Use it to read on through a page too long for one call, with the value the previous result gave.

Search the web. Returns result blocks with titles and URLs. US-only.

- `allowed_domains` / `blocked_domains` filter results.
- After answering from results, end with a "Sources:" list of the URLs you used as markdown links.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

The search turned up a few relevant points. The 398-day limit applies to publicly trusted TLS certificates issued on or after September 1, 2020, and Chromium rejects certificates that exceed it with ERR_CERT_VALIDITY_TOO_LONG. Chrome treats those certificates as misissued, so the error is a validity rule rather than a fault in the site's trust chain. Certificates issued before the enforcement date won't be impacted, neither those that have been issued from user-added or administrator-added Root certificate authorities (CAs). Chrome's per-CA scope matches that: one squid-users poster argued that the restriction covers only publicly trusted CAs, and that a private CA was not subject to it, though the thread left that unresolved. (Source: squid-users mailing list, September 2021.)

On bypassing the error, the only source I found is an Atlassian Data Center knowledge base article. It describes a workaround: With the Fisheye browser tab open, just type thisisunsafe. The text must be typed after clicking the error page body, not in the URL bar, and the browser tab will just reload and let them access the page. That article is Mac-specific, and it presents this only as a workaround. The real fix it gives is to reissue the certificate so that it is not valid for longer than 398 days.

Keep in mind that bypassing the warning skips the browser's safety check on that connection. The durable fix is to reissue the certificate with a validity period of 398 days or less. Apple's guidance is stricter: Apple recommends that certificates be issued with a maximum validity of 397 days.

Chrome rejects a certificate that lacks a matching subjectAltName entry, even when the Common Name looks right. The search results point to the same fix in several places.

- **Cause:** For Chrome 58 and later, only the subjectAlternativeName extension, not commonName, is used to match the domain name and site certificate. The error appears when the name or IP in the address bar isn't listed there.
- **IP addresses are allowed:** The certificate subject alternative name can be a domain name or IP address. So a self-signed cert for an IP needs that IP in the SAN, not only in the CN.
- **Fix:** Reissue the certificate with the hostname or IP in the SAN field. One TrueNAS forum answer adds that the cert needs to have the IP (or hostname--whatever you're entering in the browser's address bar) included in the subjectAlternativeName field as well. The CA's own common name doesn't matter.
- **Trust is separate:** The SAN fix addresses name matching only. The CA also has to be trusted by the browser, and a forum user's setup that worked in Edge suggests that part was already in place for them.

Sources: TrueNAS community threads (several copies of the same post) and TIBCO Spotfire support documentation. I didn't find an official Chromium or Google page in these results, so the Chrome 58 detail comes from secondary sources.

The search turned up Apple's own requirements page, which confirms the 825-day limit, but nothing in the results confirms a self-signed exception.

- **The 825-day rule:** Apple's support document says TLS server certificates must have a validity period of 825 days or fewer (as expressed in the NotBefore and NotAfter fields of the certificate). It applies to certificates issued after July 1, 2019, which must also contain a serverAuth EKU.
- **Consequences:** Per Apple, connections to TLS servers violating these new requirements will fail, which can stop websites from loading in Safari on iOS 13 and macOS 10.15.
- **Self-signed exception:** None of the retrieved results describe one. A Syncthing issue says the author had not tested whether the "trust this certificate anyway" prompt overrides the limit. A later user report says Safari works once a self-signed certificate is force-accepted, but that is a manual override, not a documented exception.
- **Other requirements:** Apple's page also requires SAN DNS names, so CN-only names are no longer trusted, and RSA keys of at least 2048 bits with SHA-2 signatures.
- **Later changes (unverified):** A pfSense comment claims that from September 2020 the limit dropped to about 13 months (397 days). I did not confirm that against an Apple source, so check current Apple documentation before relying on it.

RFC 6455 section 4.1 covers the case where the server names a subprotocol the client never offered. A GitHub discussion quotes the rule: if the response includes a Sec-WebSocket-Protocol header naming a subprotocol absent from the client's handshake, the client must fail the connection (the server has indicated a subprotocol not requested by the client). The same discussion notes this mechanism is meant to make both sides agree on the subprotocol (This mechanism is intended to make both sides of connection agreed on the subprotocol.).

The reverse case, where the client asked for subprotocols and the server returns none, is less clear. A W3C bug report says RFC 6455 itself doesn't require a client to abort connection establishment in that situation, and it proposed explicit failure language. The WHATWG Fetch-based spec does require failure: a WebKit bug quotes it as failing the connection when the requested protocols are non-empty and no Sec-WebSocket-Protocol value comes back. That bug notes the WHATWG rule covers a subprotocol requested by the client, but not acknowledged by the server.

The search did not surface the RFC 6455 text itself, so the wording above comes from secondary sources. I'd check the RFC directly before relying on exact phrasing.

The MDN glossary entry for "site" covers most of what you asked, though the results said nothing about IP addresses.

**Scheme:** MDN says the scheme is only sometimes part of a site's definition. In some contexts, the scheme is also considered when differentiating sites. The stricter, scheme-aware version is the one used for SameSite cookies. This stricter definition is applied in the rules for handling SameSite cookies. Under it, http and https versions of the same host are different sites (the glossary's example is http://vpl.ca vs. https://vpl.ca).

**Registrable domain:** A site is determined by the registrable domain portion of the domain name. The registrable domain is built from the Public Suffix List. It consists of an entry in the Public Suffix List plus the portion of the domain name just before it. So support.mozilla.org and developer.mozilla.org are the same site.

**Ports:** Port is ignored for site comparisons. The glossary gives https://example.com:8080 and https://example.com as an example of sites that are considered the same site because the port number is ignored when determining the site. Origin is stricter: it encompassing the scheme, the whole domain, and the port.

**IP addresses:** The results didn't cover how IP addresses are treated for site or SameSite purposes. I'd check the WHATWG URL/HTML specs or the MDN SameSite cookies page directly for that.

The search didn't return MDN's Referrer-Policy page itself. The results are from web.dev and a Google developer page, and the browser-default data is dated October 2021, so check MDN directly for current details.

- **Browser defaults:** Chrome and Firefox both default to strict-origin-when-cross-origin. Edge uses the same default, and Safari's default is similar, with some specific differences.
- **Same-origin behavior:** Among the privacy-oriented policies, strict-origin-when-cross-origin is the one that still keeps the full URL for same-origin requests. no-referrer and strict-origin never share the full URL, even for same-origin requests, so strict-origin-when-cross-origin is the better option if you need that.
- **Cross-origin behavior:** strict-origin-when-cross-origin and strict-origin only share the origin, and no-referrer shares nothing at all.
- **Private browsing exception:** Starting from version 93, for Strict Tracking Protection and Private Browsing users, the less restrictive referrer policies no-referrer-when-downgrade, origin-when-cross-origin, and unsafe-url are ignored for cross-site requests.

**Default policy:** The page lists `strict-origin-when-cross-origin` as the default:

> [`strict-origin-when-cross-origin` (default)](#strict-origin-when-cross-origin_2)
> Send the origin, path, and query string when performing a same-origin request. For cross-origin requests send the origin (only) when the protocol security level stays same (HTTPS→HTTPS). Don't send the [`Referer`] header to less secure destinations (HTTPS→HTTP).

So under the default, a same-origin request sends the full origin, path, and query string in `Referer`. For example, a navigation from `https://example.com/page` to `https://example.com/otherpage` sends `Referer: https://example.com/page`.

**Under `no-referrer`:** The page says:

> The [`Referer`] header will be omitted: sent requests do not include any referrer information.

Same-origin requests therefore send no `Referer` header at all.

Web search results for query: "browser automatically requests /favicon.ico when no link rel icon HTML spec favicon fetch behaviour Safari"

Links: [{"title":"Favicon","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Favicon"},{"title":"Open Bug 1745680 Opened 4 years ago Updated 4 months ago","url":"https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1745680"},{"title":"Open Bug 1186324 Opened 10 years ago Updated 3 years ago","url":"https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1186324"},{"title":"show bug","url":"https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=110168"},{"title":"fix 404 favicon ico error","url":"https://blog.openreplay.com/fix-404-favicon-ico-error/"},{"title":"show bug","url":"https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=258969"},{"title":"We are getting weird favicon requests only from Safari","url":"https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/698714"},{"title":"No Favicon On Safari with assets/favicon.ico","url":"https://community.plotly.com/t/no-favicon-on-safari-with-assets-favicon-ico/51992"},{"title":"[BlueOnyx:16536] Re: favicon.ico for admserv","url":"https://mail.blueonyx.it/pipermail/blueonyx/2014-November/016532.html"}]

The search didn't turn up the current WHATWG text directly, but several sources cover the behaviour and its Safari-specific wrinkles.

- **The spec allows the fallback, it doesn't require it.** An older HTML5 draft, quoted in a Mozilla bug report, says that without an icon link, browsers served over HTTP or HTTPS may try fetching /favicon.ico from the document's origin ([Mozilla Bugzilla 1186324](https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1186324)). A blog post describes the same request as built into browsers, citing the WHATWG standard ([OpenReplay](https://blog.openreplay.com/fix-404-favicon-ico-error/)). I couldn't confirm the current wording of that section.
- **Safari's behaviour differs from other browsers.** A Mozilla bug from 2021 reports that Firefox, Chrome and Safari all request the root /favicon.ico, and it notes a WebKit code bug that may explain Safari's handling ([Mozilla Bugzilla 1745680](https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1745680)). Separately, a WebKit bug says Safari 16 on macOS failed to load a `shortcut icon` link from a local HTML file, while other browsers handled it ([WebKit bug 258969](https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=258969)).
- **Safari sometimes requests favicons at unexpected paths.** One Apple developer forum thread describes Safari-only requests for /favicon.ico under sub-paths of a site, which the poster couldn't reproduce ([Apple Developer Forums](https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/698714)).

The results are mostly bug reports and forum posts rather than authoritative documentation, so the exact current Safari behaviour would need checking against WebKit source or the live spec.

Links: [{"title":"first party cookies webkit revisited","url":"https://www.simoahava.com/privacy/first-party-cookies-webkit-revisited/"},{"title":"360023003294 Cookie consent expiration in Safari 12 1 and newer","url":"https://support.cookiebot.com/hc/en-us/articles/360023003294-Cookie-consent-expiration-in-Safari-12-1-and-newer"},{"title":"Intelligent Tracking Prevention (ITP) 2.1","url":"https://docs.mapp.com/docs/intelligent-tracking-prevention-itp-21"},{"title":"Intelligent Tracking Prevention 2.1","url":"https://webkit.org/?p=8613"},{"title":"Intelligent Tracking Prevention 2.1","url":"https://webkit.org/blog/8613/intelligent-tracking-"},{"title":"WebKit Bugzilla","url":"https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=237350"},{"title":"clearcode.cc","url":"https://clearcode.cc/?p=21396"},{"title":"www.simoahava.com","url":"https://www.simoahava.com/analytics/itp-2-1-and-web-analytics/"},{"title":"Browser Cookie Updates: How Marketo/RTP Is Affected | Community","url":"https://experienceleaguecommunities-beta.adobe.com/marketo-knowledge-base-28/browser-cookie-updates-how-marketo-rtp-is-affected-246063"},{"title":"apple introduces the intelligent tracking prevention itp on all browsers in ios14","url":"https://ppc.land/apple-introduces-the-intelligent-tracking-prevention-itp-on-all-browsers-in-ios14"}]

The search turned up mostly older sources, and they conflict on whether the 7-day cap still applies to script-set cookies.

- **The original rule:** WebKit's ITP 2.1 caps persistent cookies created through document.cookie to a seven-day expiry. Cookies with shorter expiries keep them (Persistent cookies that have an expiry shorter than seven days keep their shorter expiry.).
- **Conflicting report on removal:** Simo Ahava's blog says that in a recent 2022 release WebKit stopped applying an expiry cap to JavaScript cookies, and that the restriction was folded into the general rule for script-writable storage. He says he did not confirm the exact release. Other sources still describe the cap as active, so I couldn't verify the change from WebKit's own release notes.
- **Script-writable storage:** Separately, storage such as IndexedDB, LocalStorage and Service Worker data is deleted if the site does not receive a user interaction (click, tap, or keyboard input) in 7 days of browser use.
- **Server-set cookies:** WebKit's bug tracker says the browser can't reliably tell a script-created cookie from a server-created one once it exists, apart from only servers can create HttpOnly cookies. A developer asked whether a server-set HttpOnly cookie with a 28-day expiry would be honored, and the excerpt I retrieved doesn't clearly answer that.

I didn't find a first-party cap that applies only to server-set cookies. The most reliable next step is WebKit's own release notes or the Cookie Status tool, which tracks per-browser behavior.

Links: [{"title":"- From: Mike West <mkwst@google.com>","url":"https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/public-webappsec/2015Sep/0213.html"},{"title":"WebKit Bugzilla","url":"https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=201591"},{"title":"configure content security policy with websockets and express","url":"https://outlandish.com/blog/configure-content-security-policy-with-websockets-and-express/"},{"title":"- From: André N. Klingsheim <andre.klingsheim@owasp.org>","url":"https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/public-webappsec/2015Sep/0211.html"},{"title":"support.pega.com","url":"https://support.pega.com/node/372406"},{"title":"Content-Security-Policy: connect-src directive","url":"https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/web/http/headers/content-security-policy/connect-src"},{"title":"Source code","url":"https://searchfox.org/firefox-main/source/dom/security/test/csp/test_websocket_self.html"},{"title":"https-github_com.proxy.bugsmash.io","url":"https://https-github_com.proxy.bugsmash.io/w3c/webappsec-csp/issues/7"},{"title":"Content-Security-Policy: connect-src directive","url":"https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Content-Security-Policy/connect-src"}]

The results show that `'self'` in `connect-src` covers WebSocket URLs inconsistently, so the safest approach is to list the WebSocket origin explicitly.

- **Spec behavior:** The CSP matching rules are origin-based, and the scheme is part of the origin. A WebKit bug report quotes the spec as allowing `wss` on the same host and port, and allowing `ws` only when the page itself is served over `http` ([WebKit Bugzilla](https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=201591)).
- **Browser gaps:** MDN says `connect-src 'self'` does not resolve to WebSocket schemes in all browsers ([MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Content-Security-Policy/connect-src)). The WebKit report says Chromium fixed the issue around 2018, but Safari still blocked same-host `wss` as of a February 2021 comment. I did not check Safari's current status.
- **Firefox:** A Firefox test file is titled as allowing WebSocket schemes under `'self'` (Bugzilla 1345615), and it checks both `ws:` and `wss:` ([Searchfox](https://searchfox.org/firefox-main/source/dom/security/test/csp/test_websocket_self.html)).
- **Design history:** In 2015, Mike West suggested that `'self'` could map `ws`/`wss` to the page's scheme, so `https` pages would allow only `wss` ([W3C list](https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/public-webappsec/2015Sep/0213.html)). The CSP repo issue #7 was later closed.
- **Workaround:** Add the explicit socket address, such as `ws://host:port` or `wss://host:port`, next to `'self'` in `connect-src`. One developer's example did this with helmet and noted that non-default ports must be included ([Outlandish](https://outlandish.com/blog/configure-content-security-policy-with-websockets-and-express/)).

The search results consistently put Chrome's HTTP/1.1 limit at six connections per host, but the sources are mostly older, so treat the current figure as unverified.

- **Chrome's limit:** A Taiwanese tech article says Chrome allows up to 6 TCP connections per host and cites Google's Chrome support page, though that page itself didn't appear in the results (per host, 6 connections). A 2015 article says Chrome is hard-coded to six connections per server, while Firefox defaulted to 15.
- **Historical values:** Steve Souders' 2008 roundup lists Chrome at 4 connections for version 3 and 6 from version 4 onward (Chrome 1,2 | 6 ... Chrome 3 | 4 | 4 | Chrome 4+ | 6).

content.content:
**replaceState() on the current entry:** The page says `replaceState()` "modifies the current history entry, replacing it with the state object and URL passed in the method parameters." It doesn't add an entry.

**pushState():** This page doesn't define `pushState()` directly. It only shows it in the example, which implies that `pushState()` adds a new entry. The example runs `history.pushState(stateObj, "", "bar.html")` on `foo.html`, and the page then says that "you could then use `history.state` to access the `stateObj` that was just added."

**Effect on the address bar and history:** Both methods change the displayed URL without loading the page. For `replaceState()`, the example says:

> "This will cause the URL bar to display `https://www.mozilla.org/bar2.html`, but won't cause the browser to load `bar2.html` or even check that `bar2.html` exists."

The history stack is where they differ. The example continues:

> "If the user now clicks Back again, the URL bar will display `https://www.mozilla.org/foo.html`, and totally bypass bar.html."

Because `replaceState()` overwrote the `bar.html` entry, `bar2.html` took its place, so Back skips straight from `bar2.html` to `foo.html`. If `pushState()` had been used for the second call, `bar.html` would have remained in the history.

**Summary:**

| | `replaceState(state, "", url)` | `pushState(state, "", url)` |
|---|---|---|
| Current history entry | Replaced with the new state and URL | Not replaced; a new entry is added (inferred from the example) |
| Address bar | Shows the new URL, without loading it | Shows the new URL, without loading it |
| Back button | Previous entry is unchanged; the replaced entry is no longer reachable | Previous entry is still reachable |

Both methods must use the same origin as the current URL, or they throw an exception.

The search didn't turn up the current Fetch spec or its credentials rules for WebSockets. The results were mostly old WHATWG commit logs plus one security write-up, so treat what follows as dated background.

- **Cookie header on the handshake:** A 2011 WHATWG change says the browser must send a `Cookie` header on the handshake, built from the user's cookie store for the target URL. It also says this is not treated as a "non-HTTP" API. The headers to send appropriate cookies must be a Cookie header whose value is the cookie-string computed from the user's cookie store and the URL url.
- **Cookies set by the server:** A 2011 commit says cookies the server sets during the opening handshake are applied as if received for the URL passed to the `WebSocket()` constructor. cookies set during the server's opening handshake, for the URL url given to the WebSocket() constructor. A 2010 commit also made those cookies take effect only when the connection opens, and not if the handshake fails (Make the cookies set by a WebSocket server get set sync with the 'open' event and not get set if the handshake fails.).
- **Origin checking is on the server:** A security write-up notes that WebSockets are not bound by the same-origin policy (SOP), even during the HTTP handshake. It cites RFC 6455, which says servers that only serve certain sites SHOULD verify the |Origin| field is an origin they expect. The same source describes cross-site WebSocket hijacking, where cookies with `SameSite=None` let a malicious page use an authenticated session if the server skips the Origin check.

I couldn't confirm from these results how the current Fetch/WHATWG spec defines the credentials behavior for WebSocket handshakes, so a follow-up search targeting the live WHATWG Fetch or WebSockets standard would be needed for that.

# Issue #230 facts: a web control surface on the remote port

Worktree: `/Users/sbgragent/.dispatch/worktrees/340ccb28`, base `7fe8949`. Investigation read: `notes.md`. Nothing was built, run or committed; `git status` is empty. No spike was run (see Unresolved, last item). Browser behaviour could not be tested here: no Chrome or Chromium is installed, and Safari needs a person's hands and a device.

## Settled

- The remote port answers only `/info` and `/pair` before authentication; every other path is refused unless it is under `/api/v1/`. Evidence: `src/app.rs:3026-3029` (`strip_prefix` and the `("GET", ["info"])` / `("POST", ["pair"])` arms before `authenticate`); notes §0 for the 404.
- The host certificate has no subjectAltName. Evidence: `src/adapters/remote.rs:97` (`CertificateParams::new(Vec::<String>::new())`).
- The host certificate's validity is rcgen's default, `not_after` = year 4096. Evidence: `rcgen-0.14.10/src/certificate.rs:83-85` (registry copy, version pinned in `Cargo.lock`); the tree's own comment at `src/adapters/remote.rs:91-92` says the same.

8. Frame or connection thread for the page (notes F7). The page's bytes are constant; serving them on the connection thread avoids a frame pass but is unlimited by rate window, and the pool is the only bound (notes F7). Owner's choice.
9. Connections for a cold page load (Unresolved). If a phone's Safari opens more than four unauthenticated connections, the fifth is dropped at accept (spike 22). Needs one device run with the pool counted; the plan may need a larger unauthenticated pool for static paths.
10. Acceptance run. Needs a phone on the same network, a real Safari, and a bundle signed with the stable identity (CLAUDE.md, "Platform-specific code"). This is the owner's, not runnable here.
11. Shipping items (CLAUDE.md "Adding a feature" steps 4–5): a CHANGELOG line under Unreleased, a README Layout row for `web/`, the design.md remote status section, and the amendment to `docs/remote-client.md` §4.1, §4.3 and §5.

# Issue #230 facts: a web control surface on the remote port

Worktree: `/Users/sbgragent/.dispatch/worktrees/340ccb28`, base `7fe8949`. Investigation read: `notes.md`. Nothing was built, run or committed; `git status` is empty. No spike was run (see Unresolved, last item). Browser behaviour could not be tested here: no Chrome or Chromium is installed, and Safari needs a person's hands and a device.

## Settled

- The remote port answers only `/info` and `/pair` before authentication; every other path is refused unless it is under `/api/v1/`. Evidence: `src/app.rs:3026-3029` (`strip_prefix` and the `("GET", ["info"])` / `("POST", ["pair"])` arms before `authenticate`); notes §0 for the 404.
- The host certificate has no subjectAltName. Evidence: `src/adapters/remote.rs:97` (`CertificateParams::new(Vec::<String>::new())`).
- The host certificate's validity is rcgen's default, `not_after` = year 4096. Evidence: `rcgen-0.14.10/src/certificate.rs:83-85` (registry copy, version pinned in `Cargo.lock`); the tree's own comment at `src/adapters/remote.rs:91-92` says the same.
- The host key is P-256 and `spki_sha256` is the hash of the key's SubjectPublicKeyInfo, not of the certificate. Evidence: `src/adapters/remote.rs:91` (doc), `:107-108` (`sha256_hex(&key.subject_public_key_info())`). Consequence: re-issuing the certificate over the same key (new SAN, shorter validity) leaves `spki_sha256` and the QR's `key` unchanged. The key lives in the Keychain and the certificate in `identity.json`; re-issue would need new code to write the new certificate.
- Apple's stated requirements for TLS server certificates: validity of 825 days or fewer, a DNS name in the Subject Alternative Name extension, RSA keys of at least 2048 bits, and the rules apply to certificates issued after 1 July 2019. Evidence: https://support.apple.com/103769 (fetched). The same page does not say whether they apply to a certificate the user has accepted as an exception. See Unresolved.
- Chrome's 398-day rule is named in the Chromium commit "Enforce 398-day validity for certificates issued on-or-after 2020-09-01" (https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/ae4d6809912f8171b23f6aa43c6a4e8e627de784). I read only the commit title from a search result, so it is a lead; see Unresolved.
- RFC 6455 §4.1, client rule: if the server's response includes `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` naming a subprotocol the client did not request, the client MUST fail the connection. The rule is triggered only when the header is present; the RFC says nothing about a response that omits it. Evidence: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455#section-4.1 (fetched).
- RFC 6455 §4.1, client request: a browser client MUST send an `Origin` header. Evidence: same section (fetched). The adapter does not read `Origin` (`src/adapters/remote.rs`, `read_request`, per notes F2; keys read are `authorization`, `upgrade`, `sec-websocket-key`, `content-length`).
- A token carried in `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` would be visible to the page's script. `new WebSocket(url, protocols)` takes the protocol list from script, and the negotiated value is readable from `WebSocket.protocol`. Evidence: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WebSocket/WebSocket (fetched). This rules the subprotocol option out for the "script never sees the token" claim.
- Fragments are not sent to the server: the fragment is not part of the `http`/`https` scheme syntax and does not appear in their ABNF. Evidence: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#section-4.2.5 (fetched). Consequence: a code carried after `#` never reaches the host; a code after `?` is in the request line of `GET /`.
- The default `Referrer-Policy` is `strict-origin-when-cross-origin`, which sends the path and query string in `Referer` on same-origin requests; `no-referrer` sends no `Referer`. Evidence: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Referrer-Policy (fetched). Consequence: the page's script and stylesheet requests, made while the HTML is parsed (before any `replaceState`), carry `?code=` in `Referer` unless the page sends `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`.
- `history.replaceState` changes the URL shown and replaces the current history entry; it does not add an entry. Evidence: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/History/replaceState (fetched). It does not remove the request that already carried the code (the `GET /?code=` and the subresource requests made before the script ran).
- The site used for SameSite cookies is the scheme plus the registrable domain; the port is ignored; `http` and `https` are different sites. Evidence: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/site (search snippet, not fetched in full; treat as settled for host names, see Unresolved for IP addresses).
- `maxTouchPoints` is 0 on Mac and typically 5 on phones. Evidence: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Navigator/maxTouchPoints (fetched). The same page does not cover iPad.
- `RemoteRequest` is constructed in one place: `src/adapters/remote.rs:506` (`Ok(Some(RemoteRequest {`), defined at `:360`. A grep of `src/` and `tests/` for `RemoteRequest {` finds no other literal. Adding fields is therefore not a breaking change for code in the tree.
- `PAIRING_WINDOW` is five minutes and `PAIRING_ATTEMPTS` is 3. Evidence: `src/core/action.rs:972-973`.
- `SessionView.card` is a label word, not an excerpt. Evidence: `control/src/lib.rs:645-646` ("The card's word: `CARD_WORKING`, `CARD_IDLE`, 'waiting on you', ..."). The issue's "one-line excerpt the card shows" has no field behind it in the wire view. `control/src/` contains no `last_message`.
- `last_message` exists only on the hook event (`src/ports/events.rs:24`, `src/adapters/hooks.rs:71`), not on `SessionView`. Evidence: the grep above.
- The schema-version rule in `src/core/model.rs:1-3` is stated for "workspace records" serialized through the model. `devices.json` (`Vec<PairedDevice>`, `src/adapters/remote.rs:80-85`) is not in `model.rs`, so the text does not reach it. Whether to bump anyway is a plan call.
- `ServerInfo.capabilities` is `[String]`. Evidence: `client/Sources/SwitchboardProtocol/Info.swift:8`. A new capability string does not change the decoded type.
- The `/info` answer is not an authentication of the server. `/info` is answered before authentication (`src/app.rs:3028`), and its `spki_sha256` comes from whichever process holds the socket. A page that compares the URL's `key` with `/info` therefore detects a mismatch of address, not an impostor who answers both. The only binding of the key to the server is TLS, which a browser does not pin to the SPKI. Settled from the tree; the issue's §1 claim should say so.
- The QR is built with `qrcode::QrCode::new` (`src/ui/remote.rs:281`), which picks the version and uses error-correction level M by default (`qrcode-0.14.1/src/types.rs:102`). Its doc says it fails only when the data is too long (`qrcode-0.14.1/src/lib.rs:71-74`). A URL of about 150 to 200 bytes is far below the limit; the size was not measured.
- The pool of unauthenticated connections is 4, and a fifth is dropped at accept. Spike 22 measured this against its own pinned client: "the pool of 4 was full" and "connection was refused in 0.6 ms" (`spikes/22-remote-port/README.md:79-83`). The spike did not use a browser.

## Unresolved

- Safari and a self-signed certificate with no SAN and a 4096 `notAfter`: whether Safari offers a click-through at all, and whether an exception persists. Tried: Apple's requirements page (above). It states the rules but not their scope for user-accepted exceptions. A search turned up a Syncthing report and a forum post, both anecdotal. Needs a device.
- Whether the 825-day and DNS-SAN rules bind the user's exception, and whether they apply to an IP-address host (Apple says "DNS name"). Same tried; no primary source settles it.
- Chrome and the 398-day rule: whether `ERR_CERT_VALIDITY_TOO_LONG` is bypassable for a self-signed private certificate. Tried: a search. The Chromium commit title is the only primary lead; a squid-users thread says private roots are exempt, unresolved in that thread. A Chrome test is not possible here (no Chrome installed).
- Chrome and missing SAN: whether a CN-only certificate for an IP is bypassable. Tried: a search. Only TrueNAS and vendor forum posts say it is refused, and they are not evidence. Chrome 58 claim not fetched from a primary source.
- Protocol negotiation when the client requested a subprotocol and the server returns none: WHATWG (as quoted in WebKit bug 271122, `https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=271122`) says fail; RFC 6455 does not. Not needed if the subprotocol option is dropped; the lead is recorded.
- Whether a browser sends its cookies on the WebSocket handshake. Tried: a search. Only 2011 WHATWG commit logs (`https://lists.whatwg.org/pipermail/commit-watchers-whatwg.org/2011/013056.html`) and a security write-up. Lead only. The current Fetch and WebSockets text was not fetched.
- `SameSite=Strict` with an IP-address host: whether two pages on different host names on the same network are "same-site" for the cookie. The MDN site glossary says nothing about IP addresses. Open. Consequence if different host names are cross-site: a page on another name cannot send the cookie under `Strict`. Still needs the WHATWG URL/site definition for IP hosts.
- Whether `Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict` cookies set after a click-through are stored and sent in Safari and Chrome. Not found in any source read. Needs a device or a fetched browser source.
- Whether iOS Safari keeps a `Max-Age` server-set cookie across relaunches and for how long. WebKit ITP 2.1 (`https://webkit.org/blog/8613/intelligent-tracking-prevention-2-1/`, search snippet only) caps persistent `document.cookie` cookies at seven days; a later blog says the JS cap was removed in 2022. The two conflict and neither was verified. Needs WebKit release notes or a device.
- Whether Safari's `'self'` in `connect-src` allows `wss:` to the same host and port. MDN says `'self'` does not cover WebSocket schemes in every browser. WebKit bug 201591 (`https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=201591`) reports Safari still blocking same-host `wss` as of a February 2021 comment. Current status not checked. A plan that lists `wss://<host>:<port>` explicitly in `connect-src` does not depend on the answer; that recommendation is the plan's to make.
- Whether browsers request `/favicon.ico` by themselves and what they do with a 404. Tried: a search. Mozilla bug 1745680 (search snippet) says Firefox, Chrome and Safari request the root path. Current Safari behaviour not checked. A `<link rel="icon">` with a data URI would avoid the request but needs `img-src data:` in the CSP; not tested.
- The iPad's user agent in desktop-site mode, and whether `maxTouchPoints > 1` tells an iPad from a Mac. The MDN value is documented for Mac (0) and phones (typically 5); iPad not stated. Needs a device.
- Browser limit on concurrent connections to one host. Tried: a search. Secondary sources say 6 for Chrome on HTTP/1.1; RFC 9112 §9.4 (not fetched) says a client SHOULD NOT keep more than 2. The number that matters is how many unauthenticated connections Safari opens for `/`, a script, a stylesheet, a favicon, and the WebSocket on a cold load. Needs a device or a network trace.

- Whether `Host`-header rebinding from another origin reaches the host under a certificate exception. Not searched; the cookie argument above depends on the SameSite answer.
- Whether the Keychain-stored key and the certificate in `identity.json` can be re-issued with a SAN and a 825-day validity without changing `spki_sha256` (see Settled). The arithmetic holds; no code in the tree does it.
